keyIdeas: Cournot competition is quantity competition: each firm chooses output while taking competitors' quantities as given.
Market price is determined by total industry output.
Compared with Bertrand competition, Cournot generally produces lower aggregate output, higher prices, and higher profits.
Collusion in a Cournot setting makes firms act more like a monopolist, reducing output and increasing prices further.
Collusion is fragile because each firm has an incentive to secretly expand output while others restrict production.
Stackelberg competition is sequential: a leader commits first and a follower observes and responds.
The model differs from Bertrand competition because decisions are not simultaneous price cuts.
The leader's commitment can shape the market and give the leader a first-mover advantage.
Compared with Bertrand competition, Stackelberg outcomes tend to have lower output and higher prices.
The follower still earns positive profit, but responds within boundaries created by the leader.
Information cascades occur when people imitate observed actions instead of relying on their own private information.
Cascades require sequential decisions, private information, and inference from others' visible actions.
Positive cascades can create social proof, trend formation, and brand momentum.
Negative cascades can rapidly damage reputation when early criticism becomes a social signal.
Cascades are fragile because new credible information can reverse them.
A network effect exists when a product becomes more valuable as more users adopt the same or compatible system.
Direct network effects come from users directly increasing value for other users; indirect network effects come through complements.
Positive feedback can lead to tipping and lock-in.
Network-market firms compete to build installed base, expectations, and ecosystem strength.
Penetration pricing, promotions, partnerships, and easy access can help reach critical mass.
Durable goods provide value over time, so current sales reduce future replacement demand.
Inter-temporal price discrimination charges higher initial prices to high-willingness-to-pay consumers and lowers prices later.
The Coase conjecture says a durable-goods monopolist that cannot commit to future high prices may lose market power because buyers wait.
Firms can respond through limited availability, leasing, planned obsolescence, secondary-market control, and ecosystem lock-in.
Apple and Disney illustrate lifecycle pricing, product replacement, trade-ins, and limited availability strategies.
Vertical differentiation is based on quality: most consumers agree which product is better but differ in willingness to pay for it.
Horizontal differentiation is based on personal preference rather than a shared quality ranking.
A lower-quality position can be profitable by reducing direct price competition with premium products.
Second-degree price discrimination is a single-firm menu strategy, while vertical differentiation describes competing firms at different quality levels.
Cars, airlines, and hotel brand portfolios show how firms use quality ladders to serve different willingness-to-pay groups.
Demarketing deliberately reduces, suppresses, or redirects demand when demand is excessive or inappropriate.
It differs from reverse marketing: demarketing is firm-led demand control, while reverse marketing is consumer-led search for supply.
General demarketing reduces demand broadly, often through price increases, access limits, lower promotion, or quantity limits.
Selective demarketing filters less profitable customers and focuses resources on high-value segments.
Ostensible demarketing appears to restrict access but can increase desirability by creating scarcity and authenticity.
Exclusive territories give one distributor, retailer, or franchisee the right to sell in a specific geographic or customer area.
They reduce intrabrand competition and can encourage local advertising, service, and relationship investment.
They are a type of vertical restraint and require monitoring to prevent cross-area selling.
Exclusive territories control where retailers sell, while exclusive dealing controls what brands retailers sell.
The strategy trades off some competition for stronger channel coordination and control.
